p1.t: Be honest, Lama. What do you think of my Reading Week poster? I'd really like some constructive criticism.

dialogue.scene: Emma and Fahad are reading an article about teenagers and sleep before a class discussion.

p1.t: This article says teenagers are lazy because they sleep until noon. That's a sweeping generalisation, isn't it?
Definitely. It comes across as a bit unfair. Teenagers tend to sleep later, but there's a scientific reason for it.
Right. Our body clocks seem to shift as we grow up, so we don't feel sleepy until later at night.
That's true to some extent. But lots of us also stay up late chatting with friends.

p2.t: So, on the whole, would you say our class is sleep-deprived?
Quite a few of us appear to be, especially during exam week. Not everyone, though.
Then schools that start a bit later might actually help students concentrate.
Possibly. It seems that some schools abroad have tried it, with fairly good results.

dialogue.scene: After a family lunch in the majlis, Reem's grandfather tells her what he thinks she should study at university.

p1.t: Reem, your uncle is a doctor, and so was my father. You'd make an excellent doctor too.
Thank you, Grandad. I can see where you're coming from, but I've set my heart on architecture.
Architecture? Doctors help people every day. It's a far more useful job.
With all due respect, I'm not entirely convinced that's true. Architects seem to help people in a different way.

p2.t: How so?
Well, good buildings tend to make people healthier and happier. Think of hospitals with lots of natural light.
Hmm. I suppose I hadn't looked at it like that.

dialogue.scene: Dana and Hessa present 'Ask Dana', the advice slot on their school radio. Today a student has sent in a tricky problem.

p1.t: Welcome back! Today's message says: 'My best friend wants to read her very long poem on National Day. What should I tell her?'

Exactly. You need to strike a balance. Start with what you genuinely like about the poem.
Then you could perhaps say: 'It seems a little long for a short event. I wonder if you could choose your best verses?'

p2.t: That's tactful. It doesn't come across as criticism; it sounds like advice.
And she still gets to perform, which is what really matters to her.
So, to our listener: be kind, but be clear. That's how you get your message across.

dialogue.scene: Reem is chairing a panel on the school radio. The question is whether volunteering should be compulsory for students.

p1.t: Welcome to our panel. Today's question: should volunteering be compulsory for students? Dana, you have the floor. Please keep it brief.
Thanks. I think it should stay voluntary. If people are forced, they won't really care about the work.
Sorry to interrupt, but isn't that true of homework too? We still have to do it.
If I could just finish, homework is for our own learning, but volunteering should come from the heart.

p2.t: You both make a valid point. Lama, would you like to say more?
Yes. Going back to Dana's point, many students never try volunteering simply because nobody asks them. A few required hours could change that.
That's fair. Maybe a few hours, but students should choose the activity themselves.
So, a compromise! Let's wrap up there. Chairing this discussion was easier than I thought. Thank you both!

dialogue.focus: Sorry to interrupt, but isn't that true of homework too?

dialogue.scene: Omar is interviewing his cousin Majid, a young Arabic calligrapher, for the school magazine.

p1.t: So, Majid, when did you take up calligraphy?
About three years ago. My grandfather showed me some Thuluth script, and I was hooked.
You're clearly passionate about it. What do you love about it most?
What I love about calligraphy is the patience it needs. One wrong move and you have to start again.

p2.t: That sounds stressful! Don't take this the wrong way, but isn't it a bit boring?
Not at all. Actually, it's therapeutic. When I'm writing, I lose track of time completely.
And what makes it special compared with other kinds of art?

Some Saudi start-ups, such as the delivery app Jahez, have grown into large companies.
Programmes in Riyadh and other cities help young people turn ideas into businesses.
qs: Which app do you think people in Saudi Arabia still need?
What makes a new app catch on?

3-0.exit: Judge an app you use every day: give its main strength and its main drawback.

3-1.objective: Today you will compare and judge different solutions to traffic problems near schools.
3-1.warmup: What is the traffic like near your school in the morning?

expressions.frame: ___ is nowhere near as ___ as …

dialogue.scene: Saad and Majid from the student council are judging ideas to reduce the traffic jam outside their school every morning.

p1.t: OK, we've got three ideas to tackle the morning traffic: a school bus, staggered start times and a weekly 'walk to school' day.
The bus is the best option in the long term. It would take dozens of cars off the road.
True. It's questionable whether enough families would pay for it, though.
Fair enough. What about staggered start times? Younger classes could start fifteen minutes earlier.

p2.t: On paper, it's simple. But is it feasible? Parents with children in different years would have to come twice.
Good point. And the walking day?
It's nice, but it's only a short-term fix. One day a week is nowhere near as effective as a daily bus.
So the bus is still our strongest option. The main drawback is cost, so let's ask the school about a discount.

dialogue.focus: It's questionable whether enough families would pay for it, though.
qs: Which three ideas do Saad and Majid discuss?
Why might staggered start times not be feasible?

speakout.scene: Your town council wants ideas to reduce traffic near schools. You are judging three ideas: a school bus, a car-free zone near the gate, and online classes once a week.

prompts.q: What do you think of the school bus idea?
prompts.hint: Judge it 'in the long term' and mention one drawback.

prompts.q: And the car-free zone?
prompts.hint: Say whether it's feasible, using 'It's questionable whether …'.

prompts.q: Which idea is the weakest?
prompts.hint: Compare with 'nowhere near as … as' or call it 'only a short-term fix'.

culture.title: Around the world: School Streets
points: In some UK cities, roads outside schools are closed to cars at the start and end of the school day.
These 'School Streets' aim to cut pollution and make walking and cycling safer.
Some studies found that more children walked or cycled to school after the change.
qs: Would a 'School Street' work outside your school? Why or why not?
How do most students at your school get there?

3-1.exit: Judge two ways of getting to school, by car and by bus, using 'far more … than' and 'in the long term'.

3-2.warmup: What does your school or family do to save water or electricity?

dialogue.scene: Emma and Reem from the eco club have money for one green project at their international school in Jeddah.

p1.t: We've got a budget for one green project. Let's weigh up the two options: solar panels or water-saving taps.
Solar panels make so much sense here. We have sunshine almost every day.
True, but the upfront cost is huge. It could take years before they pay off.
In the long term, though, the benefits outweigh the costs. The school's electricity bill would drop.

p2.t: Maybe. But water-saving taps are far cheaper and much more cost-effective in the short term.
That's a fair point. Their main drawback is that students might not even notice them.
That's exactly why we'd need posters too. Water is precious in a desert country.
OK. It remains to be seen whether the head will agree, but let's present both options.

dialogue.focus: In the long term, though, the benefits outweigh the costs.
qs: What two options is the eco club considering?
Why is Emma worried about the solar panels?

speakout.scene: Your school has money for one green project: a vegetable garden, recycling bins in every classroom, or solar-powered lights for the playground. Judge the options.

prompts.q: Which option is the most cost-effective?
prompts.hint: Compare the costs, using 'cost-effective' or 'upfront cost'.

prompts.q: Would the garden really be worth the effort?
prompts.hint: Use 'In the long term, the benefits outweigh …' or 'It remains to be seen whether …'.

prompts.q: So which one would you choose?
prompts.hint: Weigh up the options and give a final judgement with a reason.

culture.title: Around Saudi Arabia: The Saudi Green Initiative
points: The Saudi Green Initiative was launched in 2021.
One of its goals is to plant ten billion trees across the country over the coming decades.
It also aims to protect land and sea areas and to increase the use of renewable energy.
qs: Which green project would you like to see in your city?
Do the benefits of planting trees in the desert outweigh the costs? Why?

3-2.exit: Judge one green idea for your home: say whether the benefits outweigh the costs, and why.

3-3.objective: Today you will give a balanced judgement on using AI tools for schoolwork.
3-3.warmup: Have you ever used an AI tool to help you learn? What did you use it for?

expressions.def: after thinking about all the facts

expressions.def: people haven't decided yet if something is good

expressions.def: something with both good and bad effects

dialogue.scene: Lama asks her older cousin Sara, a university student, what she thinks about using AI chatbots for homework.

p1.t: Some of my classmates use AI chatbots for all their essays. Is that such a bad thing?
Honestly, AI is a double-edged sword. It can explain things brilliantly, but it can also become a shortcut.
A shortcut to what?
To good marks without real learning. If you rely on it for everything, you never build critical thinking.

p2.t: But it's debatable whether teachers can even tell the difference.
Maybe not, but you'll notice the difference in your exams, when there's no chatbot to help.
Fair enough. So should students avoid it completely?
Not at all. The jury is still out, but on balance, I'd use it as a tutor, not a writer.

dialogue.focus: Honestly, AI is a double-edged sword.
qs: Why does Sara call AI a double-edged sword?
How does Sara think students should use AI?

speakout.scene: Your school is deciding whether to allow AI tools in class. You are on the student panel and must judge the idea.

prompts.q: What's the biggest advantage of allowing AI in class?
prompts.hint: Give one clear advantage and an example.

prompts.q: And the biggest risk?
prompts.hint: Use 'a double-edged sword' or 'The main drawback is …'.

prompts.q: So, on balance, should the school allow it?
prompts.hint: Start with 'On balance, …' and add a condition.

culture.title: Around the world: AI in the Classroom
points: Schools around the world are trying to decide how students should use AI tools.
Some schools ban them for homework, while others teach students to use them responsibly.
Many teachers now ask students to explain their thinking aloud, which AI cannot do for them.
qs: Should students be taught how to use AI at school? Why?
Which school skills will still matter most in a world with AI?

3-3.exit: Give a balanced judgement, in two sentences, on using calculators in maths lessons.

dialogue.scene: Turki and Sam, the class representatives, must decide how to spend the money left in the class fund.

p1.t: We've got 3,000 riyals left in the class fund. We need to narrow down the ideas to one.
Let's rule out the new football kit. Only half the class plays football, so it's hard to justify.
Agreed. That leaves the trip to the science centre and the class party.
The party would be fun, but it's over in three hours. The trip is by far the best value for money.

p2.t: True. We'd learn something and still have fun. The main drawback is transport.
The school bus is free if we book early, so that's not really a problem.
Perfect. Then the benefits clearly outweigh the drawbacks. Let's go for the trip.
Great. I'm sure it'll be worth every riyal.

dialogue.focus: The trip is by far the best value for money.
qs: Why do they rule out the football kit?
Why does Sam prefer the trip to the party?

speakout.scene: Your family has 2,000 riyals to spend on something for everyone: a weekend trip, a new TV, or a family membership at a sports club. Help them decide.

prompts.q: Which option would you rule out first, and why?
prompts.hint: Use 'I'd rule out … because …'.

prompts.q: Which option is the best value for money?

culture.title: Around the world: Learning to Budget
points: In many countries, teenagers receive a regular allowance so that they can practise managing money.
Many experts suggest a simple rule: save part of your money before you spend the rest.
Comparing prices and asking 'Do I really need this?' helps people avoid wasting money.
qs: Do you save part of your money? Why or why not?
Should schools teach students how to manage money? Why?

3-4.exit: Judge something you bought recently: was it good value for money? Explain why.

dialogue.scene: Hamad and Leo are judges at their school's Innovation Challenge. Three teams have presented their projects.

p1.t: Right, let's judge the three projects against our criteria: originality, cost and how practical they are.
The drone that delivers books between classrooms is original, but it seems a bit far-fetched.
I agree. It's debatable whether it would be safe in crowded corridors.
The smart water bottle is clever, but the main drawback is the price. Each one costs 200 riyals.

p2.t: So that leaves the app for reporting broken things around the school.
It's simple, but it stands up to scrutiny. It's cheap, practical and easy to use.
Then it's by far the strongest project. Are we ready to reach a verdict?
Yes. The app comes out on top. Let's announce it!

dialogue.focus: It's debatable whether it would be safe in crowded corridors.
qs: What are the judges' three criteria?
Why do the judges choose the app?

speakout.scene: You are a judge at your school's Innovation Challenge. The teams have presented a solar-powered bench that charges phones, a 'lost and found' app and a robot that cleans whiteboards. Judge them with your partner (the teacher).

prompts.q: What criteria should we use to judge the projects?
prompts.hint: Suggest two or three criteria and explain why they matter.

prompts.q: Which project has the biggest weakness?
prompts.hint: Use 'The main drawback is …' or 'far-fetched'.

prompts.q: So, which project comes out on top?
prompts.hint: Reach a verdict with 'by far' and give two reasons.

culture.title: Around the world: 5,127 Prototypes
points: The inventor James Dyson says he built 5,127 prototypes before his bagless vacuum cleaner worked.
Each failed version helped him find and fix a problem.
His story shows that judging your own ideas honestly is part of inventing.
qs: Would you keep going after a hundred failed attempts? Why?
What criteria would you use to judge your own ideas?

3-5.exit: Choose the best invention of the last fifty years and give your verdict, with one strength and one drawback.

words.ex: Thanks for the constructive criticism; it really helped.
The dark colours come across as rather serious.
The text is a bit on the small side.
I'm not entirely sure that the title fits the topic.
You could tone down the red a little.
Your choice of photos is spot on.

dialogue.t: Be honest, Lama. What do you think of my Reading Week poster? I'd really like some constructive criticism.
Well, the photos are spot on. The bright orange, though, comes across as a bit loud to me.
Really? I thought it would catch people's attention.
It does, but it seems to pull your eyes away from the message. You could perhaps tone it down slightly.
OK, maybe a softer orange. What about the title?
It's a bit on the small side. I'm not entirely sure that people will see it from the back of the hall.

grammar.title: Softening criticism
grammar.ar: نخفّف النقد بكلمات مثل a bit / slightly / a little وبعبارات مثل It seems … و I'm not entirely sure that …

I'm not entirely sure that the ending works.

words.ex: Teenagers tend to go to bed later than adults.
On the whole, our class gets too little sleep.
I agree with you to some extent, but not completely.
'All teenagers are lazy' is a sweeping generalisation.
Many students are sleep-deprived during exam week.
I stayed up late to finish my science project.

dialogue.t: This article says teenagers are lazy because they sleep until noon. That's a sweeping generalisation, isn't it?
Definitely. It comes across as a bit unfair. Teenagers tend to sleep later, but there's a scientific reason for it.
Right. Our body clocks seem to shift as we grow up, so we don't feel sleepy until later at night.
That's true to some extent. But lots of us also stay up late chatting with friends.
So, on the whole, would you say our class is sleep-deprived?
Quite a few of us appear to be, especially during exam week. Not everyone, though.

grammar.title: tend to and seem to

dialogue.t: Reem, your uncle is a doctor, and so was my father. You'd make an excellent doctor too.
Thank you, Grandad. I can see where you're coming from, but I've set my heart on architecture.
Architecture? Doctors help people every day. It's a far more useful job.
With all due respect, I'm not entirely convinced that's true. Architects seem to help people in a different way.
How so?
Well, good buildings tend to make people healthier and happier. Think of hospitals with lots of natural light.

Come on, it'll only take five minutes!
I know, but if Mr Ali noticed, we'd both be in a tricky position. It seems a bit risky to me.
Fair enough. I just don't understand question four at all.
Well, I'm happy to lend a hand with that. Shall we go through it together at break?

grammar.title: Declining politely

I'd rather not, if that's OK.
I can't this weekend, but how about next Thursday?

Sure. Is everything OK?
Well, this is a bit awkward, but it seems that we've fallen behind with the slides, and the deadline is on Thursday.
Ah. Yes, I haven't started my part yet. I've had football training every evening.
I understand. But I'm not entirely sure that Omar and I can finish everything alone. I wonder if you could do your slides by Tuesday.
That's fair. I know I haven't been pulling my weight lately.

grammar.title: Raising a problem politely

It seems that some of the work hasn't been done.
I wonder if you could finish your part by Tuesday.

words.ex: It was very tactful of you not to mention her mistake.
My brother is so blunt that he sometimes upsets people.
I didn't mean to hurt your feelings.
Stop beating around the bush and tell me.
You need to strike a balance between honesty and kindness.
A short example helps you get your message across.

dialogue.t: Welcome back! Today's message says: 'My best friend wants to read her very long poem on National Day. What should I tell her?'
Tricky! If you're too blunt, you might hurt her feelings. But if you beat around the bush, she won't understand.
Exactly. You need to strike a balance. Start with what you genuinely like about the poem.
Then you could perhaps say: 'It seems a little long for a short event. I wonder if you could choose your best verses?'
So, to our listener: be kind, but be clear. That's how you get your message across.
Keep your messages coming, everyone. See you next week!

Sorry to interrupt, but who's bringing the tent? Last time we forgot it.
Good point. My uncle has a big one. Anyway, after dinner we'll—
Can I just add something? The weather app says it might get really cold after midnight.
Ah. OK, so everyone needs warm blankets. As I was saying, after dinner we'll watch the stars.
Could I come in here? Last time we all talked over each other and nobody decided anything.
True! Let's take turns this time. I'll chip in with snacks and my telescope.

Taif again? We went there last year!
Hold on a second, Yousef. If I could just finish, I've got two other ideas too.
Go on, Lama. Bear with her, Yousef.
Thanks. As I was saying, Taif is cooler. The second option is Al-Baha, and the third is the Red Sea coast.
The Red Sea! Now you're talking. Sorry I kept interrupting.

Can I just add one more thing? We could use bean bags instead of hard chairs.

Sorry, guys, we're getting sidetracked. That's interesting, but it's a bit off the point.
Fair enough. Where were we?
Going back to what Sam said about the moon, that's a good idea. A night with no moon means darker skies.

Thanks. I think it should stay voluntary. If people are forced, they won't really care about the work.
Sorry to interrupt, but isn't that true of homework too? We still have to do it.
If I could just finish, homework is for our own learning, but volunteering should come from the heart.
You both make a valid point. Lama, would you like to say more?
Yes. Going back to Dana's point, many students never try volunteering simply because nobody asks them. A few required hours could change that.

A shortcut to what?
To good marks without real learning. If you rely on it for everything, you never build critical thinking.
